note: CLOSED 2026-09-08, and the finding was HALF WRONG in the worse direction. routes/auth.ts:1136 never reaches loadErrorMessage: sign-in goes through auth-context.tsx:939, which prefers errBody.message, so a DATABASE OUTAGE renders as literally "Invalid credentials." — telling users their password is wrong while the database is down, the exact lie AUTH-02 exists to stop. Fixed by widening the contract: a body-level code would have been dead on arrival (all ten callers hand a bare Response to a SYNCHRONOUS classifier and never read the body), so the discriminator is an X-Auth-Reason HEADER mirrored into the body, with exposure added at the error-localization onSend chokepoint because server.ts declares no exposedHeaders and the browser would otherwise drop it. title: A wellness session can be oversold: capacity is counted, then created, with nothing in between
note: CLOSED 2026-09-09 in 7e855343 with a lock, not a constraint — as the finding said, a count ceiling is not index-shaped. enrollUnderCapacityLock (routes/wellness-sessions.ts:156) opens one transaction, takes pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(key, 0)) on a per-session key, then counts held enrolments and creates inside that transaction, so two concurrent enrolments serialise on the session instead of both reading the same count. BOTH enrolment paths go through it — free (:571) and paid (:632) of POST /sessions/:id/enroll, traced 2026-09-12. The count at :603 is a deliberate cheap pre-check before razorpay.orders.create so a provably-full class never mints a live order; the authoritative re-count is under the lock. A transaction-scoped advisory lock releases at COMMIT, so it holds under Supabase's transaction-mode pooler where a session-scoped one would not. WHAT THE TEST DOES AND DOES NOT PROVE: wellness-enroll-capacity.f455.test.ts mocks Prisma and models the advisory lock as a per-key mutex, then fires six concurrent enrolments through the real route. It proves the route takes the lock and that count-then-create is serialised under that model; by its own header it does not prove Postgres blocks a second backend. No run against a real database was made. At that cadence — health smoke twice a day, daily fleet run once — production is rebuilt ~90 times a month for markdown: at the measured 3.5 min median that is ~315 deploy-minutes, 63% of the 500 build-minute budget in docs/free-tier-budgets.md, before any real deploy (deploy wall time includes non-build phases, so these are upper bounds on build minutes). title: Production API starts with tsx from source — a dashboard Start Command overrides render.yaml, so migrate deploy never runs and dist/ is never executed
note: [2026-10-06 status] OPS-19: dashboard Start Command still overrides render.yaml per the 2026-09-12 measurement, so migrations apply by hand; the prod-db-task workflow (this PR) is the sanctioned way to run reviewed SQL meanwhile. | MEASURED 2026-09-09 and 2026-09-12 (render-diag mode=detail). The Render dashboard Start Command for the API is `pnpm --filter @poojly/api exec tsx src/server.ts`. render.yaml declares `pnpm --filter @poojly/api start`, and apps/api/package.json's start is `prisma migrate deploy && node dist/server.js`; neither is used. (1) Migrations never run on deploy — the mechanism behind OPS-17's measurement that deploys leave the schema unmoved. With OPS-18, any push to main can ship code ahead of the schema it needs. (2) The dashboard build compiles dist/ with tsc and nothing ever runs it: production executes TypeScript through a dev transpiler on a free-plan instance. Boot time and memory cost were NOT measured. The dashboard also disagrees with render.yaml on region (singapore vs oregon) and autoDeploy (yes vs false), so render.yaml is descriptive, not authoritative, for this service. DO NOT just paste render.yaml's command into the dashboard: that switches on migrate-on-boot (a failing migration then fails the deploy) and runs `node dist/server.js`, a path production has never executed. Boot the dist build once somewhere safe first. Owner: dashboard setting.
